headline: Two Terminal Commands That Push Mac Key Repeat Past the GUI Limit
lede: Every Mac ships with a keyboard setting that governs how quickly a held key fires repeatedly — and how long before it starts. macOS's System Settings panel exposes sliders for both, but they stop well short of the minimum the operating system actually supports. Two `defaults write` commands in Terminal unlock values the graphical interface simply will not show you.
body:
When you hold down a key, macOS fires the character repeatedly after an initial pause. Two integers govern this behavior: **KeyRepeat**, the interval between successive firings (smaller means faster), and **InitialKeyRepeat**, the delay before the first repeat triggers (smaller means less waiting). Both live in the system's global preferences domain — a master store that applies across every app unless an individual application overrides it.

The commands `defaults write -g KeyRepeat -int 1` and `defaults write -g InitialKeyRepeat -int 10` write directly to that global domain, bypassing the graphical sliders. The `-g` flag is shorthand for *NSGlobalDomain*, macOS's catch-all preferences namespace. System Settings' sliders stop at a KeyRepeat minimum of 2 and an InitialKeyRepeat minimum of 15; these commands reach 1 and 10 respectively — values the GUI refuses to offer.

The practical effect is a keyboard that feels nearly instantaneous under sustained key presses. Arrow-key navigation through large files, clearing long terminal lines, or any workflow relying on held keys all become noticeably snappier. Most apps pick up the new values on relaunch; a full logout-and-login is the safest way to propagate the change system-wide, as it flushes the in-memory preferences cache and ensures the stored value wins.

To revert, adjusting the GUI sliders will overwrite the custom values, or `defaults delete -g KeyRepeat` and `defaults delete -g InitialKeyRepeat` remove the keys entirely and restore system defaults. The `defaults` interface writes to `.plist` files in `~/Library/Preferences/`, the same backing store System Settings reads — so either path edits the same underlying record.

concepts.definition: A macOS preference integer that controls the interval between successive character firings when a key is held down. Lower values produce a faster repeat rate. The GUI minimum exposed in System Settings is 2; the terminal can write 1.
A macOS preference integer that sets the delay before repeating begins after a key is first pressed and held. Lower values shorten the wait. The GUI minimum is 15; the terminal can write 10.

The global preferences namespace in macOS, addressed as `-g` in the `defaults` command. Settings written here apply across all applications unless a specific app overrides them with its own domain values.

A macOS command-line tool for reading, writing, and deleting user preference values stored in `.plist` files under `~/Library/Preferences/`. It exposes settings that System Settings either hides entirely or limits through constrained sliders.

fact_check: The commands are valid, but there is a prerequisite the tweet omits. On modern macOS, pressing and holding a key by default opens an accent-character picker rather than repeating the character — a behavior controlled by the separate key `ApplePressAndHoldEnabled`. If that setting is active (the factory default on many Macs), KeyRepeat and InitialKeyRepeat have no effect until repeating is re-enabled with `defaults write NSGlobalDomain ApplePressAndHoldEnabled -bool false`. Users who have never changed this setting may find the tweet's commands appear to do nothing without that prior step.
